title: A Shabbat review
hookLine: what worked and what didn't over several Shabbatot
tomorrow: a month to get ready for the holy days. what goes in it?

cards: Clear out a closet and the question is always the same: keep, or toss? And what stays is usually what you can still feel: the sweater that's soft, the jacket that still smells like a trip.
After several Shabbatot, the same question comes. Songs, no phone, a slow walk, a nap, the morning portion, the candle at the end. What do you keep, and what do you drop?
The Talmud offers an unexpected test: follow your senses.

teach.h: A SOUND, A SIGHT, A SMELL.
teach.b: In Berakhot, the Talmud names three things that restore a person's spirit: a sound, a sight, and a smell. Not an idea, not an achievement. Something the body takes in.
That's a useful lens for a Shabbat review. Skip the scorecard of what slipped.

teach.h: WHAT CAME BACK DURING THE WEEK?
teach.b: Ask instead: which sound came back to me during the week? A hum at the table. Which sight?
A flame of many wicks, a quiet room. Which smell? Spices, bread, soup on the stove.
The practice that restored you is the one to keep, because it's already working. Then the Talmud adds a warning that every new habit needs.

teach.h: GRASP A LITTLE, AND YOU HOLD IT.
teach.b: Grasp too much, and you've grasped nothing; grasp a little, and you hold it. So a Shabbat review isn't a test you pass by doing everything.
You keep one or two things that restored you, do them well, and let the rest wait. Next season you can add one.
Nobody is asked to keep the whole day at once, and the days that went badly still taught you something: what doesn't fit yet.
Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud's list of what restores the spirit is a sound, a sight and a smell.
That's fifteen days of Shabbat, lived: a choice, a Friday, guests, Torah at the table, songs, a drawer, a walk, a table for one, children, friends, delight, a nap, a morning, a flame.

how: People growing into Shabbat may add one practice at a time, such as candles, a family dinner or a phone-free afternoon, and look back every few weeks at what is working before adding more.

o: a weekly class that tests what you know about Shabbat
looking back over several Shabbatot to keep what worked
the Torah reading that reviews the week's portion

s: the Talmud names a sound, a sight and a smell as things that restore the spirit
keeping more Shabbat practices at once is always the better choice
the Talmud warns: grasp too much and you've grasped nothing.
a Shabbat review means listing everything you got wrong
it starts from what restored you, and keeps that.

games.q: your friend tried Shabbat for a month: candles, no phone, a long service, a big dinner. she's exhausted and ready to quit. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: keep the one practice that restored her most, and build from there.
push through all of it; the tiredness will pass in time.
drop all of it now and try again next year.
games.why: grasp a little and you hold it. the review keeps what restored you, by sound, sight or smell, and lets the rest wait.

practice: Find one object from a Shabbat that worked, or something like it: a candlestick, a spice jar, a cup, a book. Hold it, look at it closely, smell it if it has a smell. Let it stand for the one practice you'll keep.

wordCard.voice: A Shabbat review: looking back over several Shabbatot by sound, sight and smell, and keeping the practice that restored you.

orig.note: Hebrew: grasp too much, and you've grasped nothing. the Talmud's warning for anyone taking on too much.

carryVoice: Something to keep: keep what worked, because a little, held, beats a lot, dropped. Fifteen days, lived.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 57b (three things restore a person's spirit: a sound, a sight, a smell)
Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 4b; Yoma 80a (grasp too much and you have not grasped; grasp a little and you have grasped)
